title: Back to the wild

paragraphs.text: In one of the most remarkable reintroductions of a species that had become extinct in its native habitat, consignments of Przewalski horses regarded as the most ancient equine line still existing have been transported from France to Mongolia in central Asia. The project is part of a plan by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) to restore the world's last wild horse to its native habitat, and has been co-ordinated by the Swiss-born ecologist Claudia Feh.

The Przewalski horse is the last survivor of the Great Ice Age herds that once roamed the grasslands of Eurasia; human hunters took these animals to the edge of extinction. The horse has been recognised as a distinct species since 1879, when a Russian Pole, Colonel Nikolai Przewalski, went to Mongolia on a scientific expedition. The Colonel's greatest achievement turned out to be saving the last surviving wild horse from obscurity. When animal skins and bones were brought for examination, he recognised that some belonged to domestic horses and some to Mongol ponies, but others were different. He realised they must have belonged to the only wild horse to have escaped the mass extinction suffered by all other non-domestic horses. His find aroused huge interest among European rare-wildlife enthusiasts, but the Przewalski horse proved particularly challenging to catch, transport and domesticate, and only a few specimens made their way into zoos.

Mongolians regard the horse as man's messenger to the gods, and the takh (their name for the Przewalski horse) has sacred status reaching back thousands of years. Originally native to many countries, including Poland and Southern Russia, Przewalski horses finally vanished from the wild in Mongolia in 1969 and the only specimens were in captivity. Today, over 1,500 Przewalski horses, the descendants of just 13 captured individuals, are alive.

Over a decade ago, Claudia Feh recreated the only truly wild herd of Przewalski horses in the world using released zoo animals. They were freed first into the rugged uplands of the remote Causse Méjean, in Southern France, where they were allowed to run wild. This high-altitude area was carefully selected for its resemblance to the harsh Mongolian landscape. Feh has now taken the momentous step of reintroducing the horses into the wilds of Mongolia and trying to restore their habitat.

In the early 1990s, Feh selected 11 horses from European zoos on the basis of their genetic compatibility, and took the risky decision to let them live together freely, mate naturally and form their own social groups. It is well known that in captive communities, adult stallions may fight to the death and, on occasion, kill foals. Having devoted 6,000 hours to studying free-living horses, Feh concluded this anti-social behaviour would disappear in the wild, improving the horses' chances of survival. Her gamble paid off. She was proved right when the behaviour of her animals in France changed within two generations. Later, despite never having been in Asia before, when the horses were taken to Mongolia in 2006, they adapted quickly to their new surroundings in the 13,000 hectares they occupy next to the Khar Us Nuur National Park.

A nucleus herd of 37 horses also remains in France. This offers a genetic reservoir – one already well adapted to life in the wild – in case of disease drastically reducing numbers in Mongolia. If all goes well, the French herd will be maintained for possible reintroductions elsewhere.

The truly distinctive feature of Feh's plan is to use the Przewalski horse as the flagship species for an even more ambitious project, which she calls the 'Wild Horse Mesh'. The aims of the Wild Horse Mesh are not only to protect and re-establish the habitat of the steppe grasslands, with all their endangered plants, birds and animals, but also to enable the families who live there to salvage their traditional culture and way of life. A key element of this larger project is the exchange of knowledge between the people of the Mongolian grasslands and conservation scientists. 'At a meeting of the families with the scientists we presented them with information about biodiversity, evolution and extinction and asked them to tell us about the birds, animals and plants of the local steppe,' Feh recounts. The people had been suffering heavy losses to their animal flocks during the harsh winters, losses which they attributed to drought. However, it soon became clear that the main contributor is pasture decline due to grazing pressure.

By sharing knowledge and insights between the local people and scientists, Feh hopes that over time a system of management for the region will emerge which will meet the needs of both its people and its distinctive wildlife, of which the Przewalski horse is just one example. In this, Feh says, the Wild Horse Mesh project provides a community focus that would otherwise have disappeared, like the Przewalski horse itself. Feh's project brings to three the number of Przewalski horse reintroductions in Mongolia – as she is also participating in one near Ulaan Baatar and one in the Gobi National Park.

For the horses, which have highly developed social behaviour, learning to live together and cooperate despite competition will be vital to the success of the reintroduction programme. And this is equally true for the people, according to Feh. 'Cooperation is my favourite subject,' she says. 'It's one of the driving forces of evolution, yet studies of cooperation are largely neglected in favour of studies in competition.'
